opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to two things: where the hardest problems are, and where the biggest value is.

If you look at robotics over the past few decades, most of the success has been in very structured environments — factory lines, warehouses, places where you can control the lighting, fix the positions of objects, and program the robot to repeat the same motion thousands of times. That's important work, but in a sense it sidesteps the real challenge of intelligence. The home is the opposite. Every home is different, every kitchen is arranged differently, objects are deformable, transparent, cluttered, and people move things around constantly. If a robot can work reliably in a home, it means it has genuinely solved generalization — perception, manipulation, and decision-making in an open world. So for me as a researcher, the home is almost the ultimate test of embodied intelligence.

The second reason is about impact. Think about how much of human time goes into household labor — cooking, cleaning, tidying, caring for elderly family members. And many societies, including China, are facing aging populations and shrinking labor forces. Who is going to take care of people at home in twenty years? I believe general-purpose home robots could be one of the most meaningful technologies of our generation, comparable to the car or the smartphone, in that it changes daily life for ordinary families, not just for industry.

Of course, I'm also realistic. The home robot won't arrive overnight. The path probably goes through more constrained scenarios first — retail, pharmacies, service settings — where we can collect data, refine the models, and make the business sustainable. But the North Star, the thing that keeps me motivated, is a robot that can walk into any home and actually help. That's why I chose it.

r001.rationale: The response gives broad household applications and impact on ordinary families as a reason for choosing home robotics, presenting it as a technology with unusually wide reach.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention autonomous driving or frame home robotics as the next step extending automation from driving to household tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it started as a very personal thing before it became a research direction. I did my PhD on 3D vision, and for years I was working on things like pose estimation, point cloud understanding, object perception. The work was good, the papers were getting in, but at some point I asked myself: what is all of this for? Perception on its own doesn't change anyone's life. It only matters when something acts on it.

And when you ask "where does a robot acting on perception matter most," the answer for me was always the home. Factories already have robots. Warehouses have robots. Those environments are structured, you can bolt things down, you can control the lighting, you can fix the position of every part. The home is the opposite. Every house is different, every cup is in a different place, a child leaves a toy on the floor, the sofa is a different color. That's exactly the environment where the old approach of engineering around the problem completely breaks, and where you actually need the machine to understand the world.

So the home is, in a sense, the hardest version of the problem, and also the one with the biggest payoff. If you look at demographics in China, in Japan, in Europe, aging is coming very fast. Who takes care of the elderly? Who does the cooking, the cleaning, the picking up of things? The demand side is enormous and it's not going away. If we could build a general-purpose robot that works reliably in a home, that's not a small product improvement, that changes how people live.

There was also a timing judgment. Around 2021, 2022, I felt that several things were converging. Simulation was getting good enough that you could generate data at scale. Large models were showing that if you have enough data and a general architecture, generalization emerges. And hardware, especially dexterous hands and cheap arms, was getting to the point where a lab could actually build something. So the pieces were there, but nobody had put them together for embodied intelligence yet.

And I'll admit, part of it is just that I find it exciting. When a robot picks up an object it has never seen, in a room it has never been in, there's a moment where it feels alive. I wanted to spend the next ten or twenty years on something where the moments like that keep getting bigger. A home robot is the goal that lets me do that.

r001.rationale: The response says the home has the biggest payoff and describes broad, growing demand for help with caregiving and household tasks as a reason to pursue home robotics.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention autonomous driving or present home robotics as an extension of automation from driving to household tasks.

astra-6.text:
For me, home robots bring together a fascinating technical challenge and a very practical goal. I want robots to be useful in everyday life—to take on chores and give people more time for the things they care about.

But a home is also a difficult environment for a robot. Every home is different, objects move around, and people don’t follow a fixed routine. A robot has to understand what’s around it and adapt, rather than simply repeat a programmed motion. That combination is what draws me to the problem: developing robots that can handle that complexity while doing something genuinely useful for people.

r001.rationale: The response describes home robotics as a challenging and practical goal, but does not say it has the greatest scope.

r002.rationale: It discusses chores and home complexity, but does not frame home robots as a next step after autonomous driving or as extending automation from driving outside to home tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, home robots represent a very compelling goal because they could help people in such a direct way. We spend a lot of time on everyday tasks, and a robot that could take on some of that work would give people more time and independence.

At the same time, the home is a really challenging environment for robotics. Every home is different, objects move around, and people’s needs change. You can’t simply program a fixed sequence of actions and expect it to work everywhere. A robot needs to perceive its surroundings, understand what someone wants, and adapt. That combination—a meaningful human benefit and a deep technical challenge—is what makes the goal so appealing to me.

r001.rationale: The response cites direct help to people and technical challenges, but does not say home robotics has the greatest scope as He Wang’s reason.

r002.rationale: The response does not connect home robots to autonomous driving or describe them as extending automation from driving outdoors to tasks at home.
